---
title: "Odds and log odds"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

For a probability $p$, the [**odds**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214) and [**log odds**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214) are defined below.

We first move among probability, odds, and log odds, then compute each quantity for the observed SuperTelicity groups and distinguish their ratios.

$$
\operatorname{odds}(p)=\frac{p}{1-p},
\qquad
\operatorname{logit}(p)=\log\frac{p}{1-p}.
$$

Their interpretation is easiest to anchor in the observed SuperTelicity group probabilities.

An odds value answers a “successes per failure” question. If a group contains $s$ *in* completions and $f$ *for* completions, then its observed probability is $s/(s+f)$, its odds are $s/f$, and its log odds are $\log(s/f)$. We apply these three summaries to the observed SuperTelicity groups below.

The inverse map follows from $o=p/(1-p)$: $o(1-p)=p$, so

$$
p=\frac{o}{1+o}.
$$

```{r}
#| label: observed-odds
#| echo: true
st <- read.csv("data/supertelicity/supertelicity-cloze.csv")
st$verb_type <- factor(st$verb_type, levels = c("manner", "result"))
summary_table <- aggregate(prep_in ~ verb_type, st, mean)
summary_table$n <- as.integer(table(st$verb_type))
summary_table$successes <- as.integer(aggregate(prep_in ~ verb_type, st, sum)$prep_in)
summary_table$failures <- summary_table$n - summary_table$successes
summary_table$odds <- with(summary_table, prep_in / (1 - prep_in))
summary_table$log_odds <- log(summary_table$odds)
summary_table
```

For each verb type, the `successes` and `failures` columns make the odds calculation literal: the displayed odds equal observed *in* completions divided by observed *for* completions. The probability instead divides the same success count by all completions. Thus the probability ratio and odds ratio need not agree.

The probability ratio and odds ratio are different quantities.

```{r}
#| label: compare-ratios
#| echo: true
probability_ratio <- summary_table$prep_in[[2L]] / summary_table$prep_in[[1L]]
odds_ratio <- summary_table$odds[[2L]] / summary_table$odds[[1L]]
log_odds_difference <- diff(summary_table$log_odds)
c(probability_ratio = probability_ratio, odds_ratio = odds_ratio,
  exp_log_odds_difference = exp(log_odds_difference))
```

The result-to-manner empirical odds ratio is `r round(odds_ratio, 3)`. This says that the odds of an *in* completion are multiplied by that amount; it does not say that the probability is multiplied by the same amount.

```{r}
#| label: plot-observed-probabilities
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(summary_table, aes(verb_type, prep_in)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, color = "#1F5A85") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Verb type", y = "Observed probability of an in-completion") +
  theme_classic()
```

Log odds are unbounded and additive, which is why logistic regression uses them. Probabilities remain the scale for substantive interpretation. The [PS3 page](../problem-sets/ps3/) applies this distinction to fitted contrasts.

An odds ratio from a regression is ordinarily conditional on the other predictors in that regression. Even without confounding, that conditional odds ratio need not equal a marginal odds ratio computed after averaging over those predictors. This **noncollapsibility** is a property of odds ratios, not automatically evidence of bias.

## Recap and check

1. Does doubling probability double odds? Only at special values; the table shows a probability ratio of two and an odds ratio of about $2.667$.
2. To return from odds to probability, use $p=o/(1+o)$, not $p=1/o$.

The [logistic regression page](logistic-regression.qmd) makes a coefficient equal to a conditional log odds difference.
